The main question

Can a network learn the message rule from examples?

In Lecture 2, belief propagation derived its messages from known factors.

Today: graph neural networks, which learn the rule from examples. What can they do, and what can they not do?

Derived rules need factors; learned rules need examples.

Today's plan

One network, five questions about it

First: finishing Lecture 7, step by step (19 slides).

Each part answers one question about the same network.

Warm-up

Two ideas from earlier lectures that return today

1. On the coin chain, what does coin 2's message to coin 3 carry (Lecture 2)?
Answer. What faces 1 and 2 say about coin 3, as two numbers. Returns in Part 1, as a learned message.
2. A Markov chain runs for many steps (Lecture 4). What happens to its start?
Answer. Forgotten: the chain settles at its stationary distribution. Returns in Part 4: deep networks forget their input.

Lecture 7, finished · Where we stopped

First, we finish Lecture 7: who copies whom?

Four friends toss a coin every evening, and some of them copy a friend. We only see their notebook. Can we find who copies whom?

SoWe finish this example, then see where the idea is used today.NextWhat are the friends' real habits?
Lecture 7, finished · The true habits

The answer we hope to find: three copy links

Friend 1 tosses a fair coin. Friend 2 copies friend 1 with chance 7/8; friends 3 and 4 copy friend 2 with chances 3/4 and 5/8. The method never sees this picture.

SoA strong, a medium and a weak link.NextWhat does the notebook show?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 1 · Count

Linked friends write the same face more often

In 512 evenings, count how often each pair wrote the same face. Two friends who never copy agree on half the evenings: 256.

SoEvery pair agrees more than 256, even the three pairs with no link.NextHow do we turn "how often the same" into one number?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 2 · Measure

One score per pair: zero at half the days, larger above

Lecture 7 turned each pair's agreement into one score, its information: 0 when the pair agrees on half the days, and larger the more often the pair agrees.

SoPair 1–2 agrees most and scores highest; no link scores 0.NextHow do the six pairs rank?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 3 · Compare

The indirect pair 1–3 scores above the true link 2–4

The six scores, strongest first. Green bars are true links; grey bars are not.

SoKeeping the three strongest pairs would pick 1–3 and miss 2–4.NextWhy does pair 1–3 score so high?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 3 · Why

Two copies in a row make friends 1 and 3 agree

Q: Neither friend 1 nor friend 3 copies the other. Why do they agree on 352 of 512 days? A: Through friend 2: friend 3 copies friend 2, who copies friend 1.

SoA chain of strong copies can beat one weak direct copy.NextWhich rule avoids the indirect pair?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 4 · The rule

Take the strongest pair, unless it closes a loop

Lecture 7's greedy rule (the Chow–Liu tree): go down the list of pairs; link a pair unless its two friends are already connected; stop at three links, because four friends need three links to form a tree.

Q: Which pair will the rule skip first? A: Pair 1–3: once 1–2 and 2–3 are linked, it would close a loop.

SoOne pass down the sorted list.NextWhich pair does the rule take first?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 4 · Rule, step 1 of 4

Friends 1 and 2 score highest, so we link them

Pair 1–2 has the largest score, 0.316: link it.

SoOne link: 1–2.NextWhich pair comes next?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 4 · Rule, step 2 of 4

Friends 2 and 3 come next, and no loop forms

Pair 2–3 (0.131) joins friend 3 to friend 2.

SoTwo links: 1–2, 2–3.NextCan the rule take pair 1–3?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 4 · Rule, step 3 of 4

Pair 1–3 would close a loop, so we skip it

Friends 1 and 3 are already connected through friend 2.

SoThe indirect pair is skipped.NextWhich pair joins friend 4?
Lecture 7, finished · Step 4 · Rule, step 4 of 4

Pair 2–4 joins friend 4: three links, done

Pair 2–4 (0.032) connects friend 4. Three links: stop.

SoThe rule finds the true tree: 1–2, 2–3, 2–4.NextDoes this work on a short notebook?
Lecture 7, finished · A short notebook

With only 20 evenings, friend 4 is linked to friend 3

In 20 random evenings, pair 3–4 (0.046) came out above the true link 2–4 (0.020) by chance.

SoThe weakest link is the first to go wrong.NextHow many evenings are enough?
Lecture 7, finished · More evenings

Longer notebooks place friend 4 correctly

The same rule on notebooks of different lengths:

notebooklinks foundfriend 4
20 evenings1–2, 2–3, 3–4wrong
320 evenings, 1000 notebooksthe true tree in 93%most errors misplace friend 4
512, perfect1–2, 2–3, 2–4right
SoLong notebooks give the truth; short ones need checks.NextWhat if the true links form a loop?
Lecture 7, finished · A loop

If friend 4 copies friend 2 or friend 3, the links form a loop

Change one habit: a fair toss tells friend 4 whom to copy, friend 2 or friend 3; it copies with chance 7/8.

SoFour true links: 1–2, 2–3, 2–4, 3–4.NextWhat does the greedy rule do now?
Lecture 7, finished · A loop

The tree keeps three links and drops the true link 2–3

Pairs 2–4 and 3–4 (0.168 each) enter right after 1–2; then three links are done.

SoA tree has three links; this loop needs four.NextCan another score find all four links?
Lecture 7, finished · A loop

Scoring each pair given the others finds the four links

Lecture 7's fix: score each pair given the other friends' faces (conditional information). Unlinked pairs drop to 0.

SoExactly the four true links remain.NextWhere is learning links used today?
Lecture 7, finished · In AI today: classifiers

A spam filter can link words that appear together

  1. Friends = words of an email; notebook = emails marked spam or not.
  2. Naive Bayes: words unlinked given the class, so "free" and "money" count twice.
  3. Tree-augmented naive Bayes adds a Chow–Liu tree on the words, using information given the class.

One extra tree of links, and evidence is no longer counted twice.

Lecture 7, finished · In AI today: physics from motion

A neural network learns which balls are tied by springs

  1. Friends = moving balls; notebook = their trails.
  2. Links = hidden springs. One network guesses them; a second predicts the motion.
  3. Both train on Lecture 6's evidence lower bound, with links as hidden variables.

Neural relational inference learns the links with Lecture 6's score.

Lecture 7, finished · In AI today: coming in Lecture 12

Attention chooses new links for every sentence

  1. Friends = words of one sentence.
  2. Each word weights every (earlier) word: a soft map, computed anew for each sentence.
  3. Lecture 7: one map per notebook. Attention learns how to draw a map for each input.

Today's topic: networks that also learn what to send along the links.

1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Where we are

Part 1 builds a graph neural network from belief propagation

ProblemBelief propagation needs the factors: face probabilities and κ\kappaκ, the match probability (4 in 5). Often we have only examples.We doKeep its three parts, start, message and update; let small networks learn them.WhyThis is the network that Parts 2 to 5 question.
SoThe result is a graph neural network; we train it and test it on our chain.NextWhat is our coin model?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · The model

Our model: hidden coins in a row, each showing a face

Each coin has a hidden type, A or B (ziz_izi​), and shows one face, H or T: the observation xix_ixi​, the only thing we see. Neighbouring coins are usually the same type, so a coin's face is also a clue about its neighbours.

SoTo guess one coin, combine its own face with the faces around it.NextWhat does the best combination give on H H T H T?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Example

Belief propagation gives each coin its probability of A

Belief propagation combines all five faces and gives each coin its exact probability of A.

Coin 1 shows H, and so does its neighbour coin 2: its probability of A, 0.715, is above the 0.667 its own face alone gives.

SoGiven only examples, can a network learn this rule?NextWhere does a coin's first guess come from?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Round 0

Round 0: a coin's own face gives its first guess

Before any message, a coin knows only its own face. A shows H twice as often as B, so an H makes A twice as likely as B.

SoH starts at 0.67, T at 0.33.NextHow does a neighbour's face change the guess?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Round 1

Round 1: a neighbour's face is a second, weaker clue

Coin 1 now hears coin 2's face. Coin 2 matches coin 1 only 4 times in 5, so its H is a weaker clue; the two clues multiply.

SoAfter one round, coin 1's probability is 0.75.NextWhat happens in later rounds?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Rounds

Each round, every coin hears one coin further away

Each round repeats round 1: a neighbour's message also carries what that neighbour heard the round before, so every coin hears one more coin on each side.

SoCoin 3 hears every coin, and is exact, after two rounds; every coin after four.NextWhat does one message compute?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · One message

Coin 2's message to coin 3 adds two paths

Coin 2 may be A or B, so its message about “coin 3 is A” adds two paths.

z2z_2z2​: coin 2's hidden value; ψ\psiψ: κ\kappaκ if equal, 1−κ1-\kappa1−κ if not; φ2\varphi_2φ2​: probability of coin 2's face; μ1→2\mu_{1\to2}μ1→2​: what coin 1 sent.

SoA message sums over the sender's values.NextWhich parts make up one round?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · One round

Belief propagation has three parts: start, message, update

Look back at rounds 0 and 1 : every round on any graph uses the same three parts.

SoAll three parts are formulas fixed by the face probabilities and κ\kappaκ .NextIf we do not know κ\kappaκ, which parts can a network learn?

A graph neural network learns each part instead

Keep the rounds and the links. Replace each fixed formula by a simple part with parameters to learn. Ours has only two parameters.

1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Training

Training: practise on chains whose targets we know

Practice chains we make ourselves: belief propagation writes the targets yiy_iyi​, the exact probabilities. The gap is the mean absolute error between outputs y^i\hat y_iy^​i​ and targets.

gap(u,w)=1n∑i=1n∣y^i−yi∣\mathrm{gap}(u,w)=\dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big|\hat y_i-y_i\big|gap(u,w)=n1​∑i=1n​​y^​i​−yi​​, averaged over the practice chains

H T T with u=w=0.1u=w=0.1u=w=0.1: 13(∣0.52−0.52∣+∣0.48−0.33∣+∣0.47−0.30∣)=0.11\tfrac13\big(|0.52-0.52|+|0.48-0.33|+|0.47-0.30|\big)=0.1131​(∣0.52−0.52∣+∣0.48−0.33∣+∣0.47−0.30∣)=0.11.

SoTraining = find u,wu,wu,w with the smallest gap; then the network runs on new chains without targets.NextHow does the network know which way to move uuu and www?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Training, the rule

The rule: step the way that lowers the gap

Fix u=12u=\tfrac12u=21​, move only www; the curve is the gap on 200 practice chains. The network never sees the curve: it tries www a little up and a little down.

w ← w−η⋅gap(w+δ)−gap(w−δ)2δw\ \leftarrow\ w-\eta\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{gap}(w+\delta)-\mathrm{gap}(w-\delta)}{2\delta}w ← w−η⋅2δgap(w+δ)−gap(w−δ)​,   and the same for uuu

δ\deltaδ: trial step (0.0001); the fraction is the slope; η\etaη: learning rate (0.5). Uphill, www moves down; downhill, up.

SoEach parameter walks downhill; 400 steps on uuu and www together are the whole training.NextCan one trained network work on chains of any length?
1 · From belief propagation to learned messages · Next

Next: one trained network works on chains of any length

The network trained on 3 to 8 coins has two parameters θ=(u,w)\theta=(u,w)θ=(u,w). Can we feed it 50 coins without changing them? Look back at one layer : every coin uses the same uuu and www, and the sum takes any number of neighbours.

A chain of 50 coins needs how many sets of numbers θ\thetaθ?
Answer. One: each coin applies the same uuu and www, so θ\thetaθ never depends on the length. Whether the outputs stay accurate is a separate question .

Next: sharing the same functions also gives symmetry (Part 2).

2 · Symmetry · Where we are

Part 2 asks: does one trained network fit every graph?

ProblemWe trained on chains of 3 to 8 coins, numbered left to right.We doRenumber the coins and change the size; prove what must happen.WhyOtherwise every new graph would need new training.
SoA layer built from a sum lets one θ\thetaθ serve every numbering and size.NextWhat happens when we renumber the coins?
2 · Symmetry · Idea

Renumbering the coins must not change their outputs

No retraining. Name the coins a to e. Swap the numbers of a and c (1 and 3) and run the trained network again: coins, faces and links stay, so each probability must stay.

After the swap, which coins get a different probability of A?
Answer. No coin. Each update reads the linked coins, and the links are renamed with the coins (3–4 is now 1–4). The theorem ahead proves this for every graph.
2 · Symmetry · Definition

A relabelling gives nodes new numbers, nothing else

Our swap , written as a rule: each coin keeps its face and its links, only its number changes.

Definition. A relabelling π\piπ gives old node iii the new number π(i)\pi(i)π(i).
SoRenumbering moves each node's face and its links together; matrix form .NextWhich outputs should stay, and which should move?
2 · Symmetry · Definitions

Invariant outputs stay; equivariant outputs follow their coins

Renumber the seats in a class: the class average stays; each student keeps their own mark. Below: coins a, b, c; swap the numbers 1 and 3.

Definition. A graph-level output is invariant if renumbering leaves it unchanged. Node outputs are equivariant if each node keeps its output under its new number: y^π(i)′=y^i\hat y'_{\pi(i)}=\hat y_iy^​π(i)′​=y^​i​ (coin a: y^3′=y^1\hat y'_3=\hat y_1y^​3′​=y^​1​).
SoOur probabilities of A, one per coin, should be equivariant, like the faces.NextWhich ways of combining neighbours ignore their order?
2 · Symmetry · Lemma

Sum, mean and maximum ignore the order of neighbours

Neighbours come in no natural order: combine the same three values in two orders.

Lemma. The sum, mean and maximum do not depend on the order.
SoA new order changes neither the values nor their count.NextDoes a whole layer then ignore the numbering?
2 · Symmetry · Theorem

Theorem: a message-passing layer moves with the nodes

Renumber, then apply a layer , or the reverse.

Theorem (equivariance). For every message and update network, both paths give the same vectors (for us: the same scores).

a renumbered node keeps its neighbours, so its sum .

SoThis comes from the layer's shape, not training.NextWhat follows for many layers and graph-level outputs?
2 · Symmetry · Corollaries

Three consequences: many layers, one graph-level output, any size

  1. Many layers. Each layer keeps every output with its coin , so the whole network is equivariant.
  2. One graph-level output. Add up all final node values; a sum ignores order , so it is invariant.
  3. Any size. The same Mθ,UθM_\theta,U_\thetaMθ​,Uθ​ at every coin, so one θ\thetaθ fits every length .
SoOne θ=(u,w)\theta=(u,w)θ=(u,w), trained once, serves every graph and every numbering.NextCan extra node features break this symmetry?
2 · Symmetry · Predict first

Add each node's number as a feature: what happens?

Some tasks need a node’s place. Give each coin the input (face, its number) and a third parameter vvv: start si=u⋅xi+v⋅(number)s_i=u\cdot x_i+v\cdot(\text{number})si​=u⋅xi​+v⋅(number). Then swap the numbers 1 and 3 again.

With the feature (face, iii), do the outputs still move with the nodes?
Answer. No. Coin a’s input changes from (+1,1)(+1,1)(+1,1) to (+1,3)(+1,3)(+1,3), so its start moves from u+vu+vu+v to u+3vu+3vu+3v. With the face alone, its input is +1+1+1 under both numberings .
SoUse numbers as features only when order matters (word positions, Lecture 12).NextWhich message and update functions do people use?
2 · Symmetry · Next

Next: which message and update functions to choose?

Symmetry fixes the shape; it leaves the message and update open.

One node has 3 neighbours, another 300. Which order-free combination keeps both on one scale?
Answer. Their mean: it divides by the count, while a sum of 300 similar messages is about 100 times a sum of 3.

Next: three classic ways to weigh neighbours.

How should node 2 weigh its three friends?

3 · Three classic graph networks · Definition

Sample a few neighbours and keep the own vector apart

A popular account has millions of neighbours; average only a random few, S(i)S(i)S(i).

3 · Three classic graph networks · Definition

Learn a weight for each neighbour from both vectors

Score each neighbour from both scores; scores become weights adding to 1. Simplified from the original, which also bends the score with a leaky relu .

ProblemEach layer passes messages along one link.We doFollow coin 1's output on a chain of 20 coins.WhyWhich faces can its output use?

4 · How far a network sees · Definition

The nodes within T links form the receptive field

Problem"Reach" needs a meaning on any graph.We doMeasure distance in links.WhyDistance decides what layers use.
Receptive field NT(i)={j: dist(i,j)≤T}N_T(i)=\{j:\ \mathrm{dist}(i,j)\le T\}NT​(i)={j: dist(i,j)≤T}: nodes within TTT links of iii; dist\mathrm{dist}dist: links on a shortest path.

4 · How far a network sees · Theorem

After T layers, a node sees only T links far

ProblemDoes it hold on every graph?We doState it for all networks.WhyDepth then limits reach.
Theorem (receptive field). In every message-passing neural network (MPNN), node iii after TTT layers uses only inputs within TTT links .

one layer, one link.

SoCoin 5, two layers: coins 3 to 7.NextWhich output is best?
4 · How far a network sees · Corollary

On a tree, the best T-layer output is T rounds of BP

ProblemTTT layers see only nearby coins.We doFind the best output from them.WhyNo training can beat it.
Corollary (tree). On a tree (no loops; our chain is one), let yiy_iyi​ be the exact probability of coin iii given the faces within TTT links, which TTT rounds of belief propagation compute. Any TTT-layer message-passing network, whatever its parameters, has average cross-entropy loss ≥\ge≥ that of yiy_iyi​. Proof: . With loops the tree step fails and belief propagation itself can fall above the floor .

use the TTT links perfectly; the faces beyond them are out of reach.

SoIts error is the floor.NextHow large is this floor?
4 · How far a network sees · Why the floor falls

Each extra layer about halves the error floor

ProblemHow much do the coins beyond TTT links still matter?We doMeasure the gap of TTT rounds of belief propagation on 400 chains of 20 coins.WhyProposition. If coin jjj leans to A by δ\deltaδ (probability 12+δ\tfrac12+\delta21​+δ), coin j+kj+kj+k leans by (2κ−1)k⋅δ(2\kappa-1)^k\cdot\delta(2κ−1)k⋅δ .

Left: one link, both paths counted: κ(12+δ)+(1−κ)(12−δ)=12+(2κ−1)δ\kappa(\tfrac12+\delta)+(1-\kappa)(\tfrac12-\delta)=\tfrac12+(2\kappa-1)\deltaκ(21​+δ)+(1−κ)(21​−δ)=21​+(2κ−1)δ; with κ=0.8\kappa=0.8κ=0.8 the lean keeps 0.6, and the next link acts on that new lean, so kkk links keep 0.6k0.6^k0.6k. Right: 400 chains of 20 coins; TTT rounds of belief propagation against the exact probability, mean absolute difference.

SoEach link keeps 0.6 of the lean, so each extra layer reaches coins that matter 0.6 times less; measured, the floor falls by about ×0.5 per layer.NextShould we just stack more layers?
4 · How far a network sees · The cost of depth

Repeated averaging makes all nodes nearly equal

ProblemMore layers see further . Why not 100 layers?We doWatch the simplest layer, score ← mean of itself and its neighbours, applied 40 times to 9 coins.WhyEach averaging mixes a coin with its neighbours; after many, all coins hold nearly the same score, and the outputs can no longer tell them apart.

9 coins in a chain, H = +1, T = −1, one bar each.

SoThe spread (range: tallest minus lowest bar) falls from 2 to 0.083: oversmoothing. This is the first price of too many layers; the second is on .NextHow fast does the spread shrink?
4 · How far a network sees · Theorem

The spread shrinks by one fixed factor every round

ProblemHow fast do differences vanish?We doPlot it on a log scale.WhyA fixed factor gives a straight line.
Theorem (oversmoothing). On a connected graph with self-loops, the spread after ttt rounds is at most C⋅λ2 tC\cdot\lambda_2^{\,t}C⋅λ2t​, with λ2<1\lambda_2<1λ2​<1 fixed by the graph: after the first rounds it shrinks by about λ2\lambda_2λ2​ each round .

differences fade steadily.

SoHere it is 0.953, as in Markov-chain mixing .NextDoes depth have a second cost?
4 · How far a network sees · The cost of a fixed vector

Far information must squeeze into one fixed vector

ProblemAfter TTT layers, all a node knows about the nodes within TTT links sits in its one vector of fixed size: ours one score, the bigger network 16 numbers.We doCount the nodes within 3 links on a tree with 3 neighbours per node.WhyThe count grows with TTT; the vector does not.
Observation (Alon and Yahav, 2021). Where far nodes matter, networks fail even to fit the training data.
So22 faces must fit into one score or 16 numbers, so far faces are crushed: over-squashing, the second price of depth . A chain has only 2T+12T+12T+1 such nodes, so our chain barely suffers.NextHow do networks ease both costs?
4 · How far a network sees · Remedies

Five fixes keep far information from fading

ProblemDepth averages; a fixed vector squeezes.We doChange the update or the graph.WhyFar information must arrive without fading.
SoOur network re-adds its own observation u⋅xiu\cdot x_iu⋅xi​ in every layer: a form of the first fix.NextCan enough reach tell all graphs apart?

Colour refinement compares computation trees quickly

ProblemComputation trees double each layer: too big to compare.We doRound 0: colour = face. Each round, write down for every node its colour and how many neighbours of each colour it has; nodes with the same note get the same new colour, different notes different colours.WhySame colour after ttt rounds ⇔\Leftrightarrow⇔ same tree of depth ttt.
roundnodeits colourits neighbours’ coloursnew colour
1path, end nodefone fd
1path, middle nodeftwo fe (differs from d: a different pair)
1ring or triangle, any nodeftwo fe, the same for all 12 nodes
Definition. Weisfeiler–Leman (WL) colour refinement: ci(t+1)=new(ci(t), {cj(t):j∈N(i)})c^{(t+1)}_i=\mathrm{new}\big(c^{(t)}_i,\ \{c^{(t)}_j: j\in N(i)\}\big)ci(t+1)​=new(ci(t)​, {cj(t)​:j∈N(i)}); new is a lookup table (an injective map): each distinct pair gets its own colour name, e.g. the next unused letter .

5 · What a network can tell apart · Theorem

Equal colours force equal network vectors

ProblemIs refinement a limit?We doCompare colours and vectors by layer.WhyBoth read the same inputs.
Guarantee (Xu et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2019). Nodes with equal colours after ttt rounds get equal vectors after ttt layers, in every message-passing network .

colours bound what networks see.

SoBoth graphs: one colour, one output.NextWhich networks reach this limit?
5 · What a network can tell apart · Theorem

A sum keeps counts; a mean or a maximum loses them

ProblemRefinement’s note counts neighbours of each colour. Which way of combining messages keeps those counts?We doNode iii has neighbours {1, 1}; another node has {1}. Combine by mean, max and sum.WhyIf the combination loses the count, two nodes with different notes get the same vector.
Guarantee (Xu et al., 2019). If a layer sums the neighbours’ vectors (encoded so that the sum identifies the multiset) and its update is one-to-one (distinct inputs give distinct outputs, like new ), then after ttt layers two nodes have equal vectors exactly when they have equal colours. Such a layer, hi′=MLP((1+ϵ) hi+∑j∈N(i)hj)h_i^{\prime}=\mathrm{MLP}\big((1+\epsilon)\,h_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}h_j\big)hi′​=MLP((1+ϵ)hi​+∑j∈N(i)​hj​), is the graph isomorphism network (GIN) .
SoOnly the sum separates them. Ours sums too, but its linear update is not one-to-one.NextWhy did loopy belief propagation fail too?

Loopy belief propagation also runs on the tree

ProblemLoopy belief propagation failed too.We doUnroll its messages ; exact: sum over the 8 cases; our network: the rule of .WhyIts computation tree repeats each coin's evidence.
SoOn the 3-coin ring of the midterm, loopy belief propagation overshoots; our network lands closer to the exact probability. Two different limits: on a given ring the network can be more accurate than belief propagation, yet neither can tell the ring from the triangles .NextWhich extra input reveals the loop?

7 · One application: Sudoku · The graph

Sudoku is a graph: cells linked by row, column and box

Rule: every row, column and box holds each digit exactly once (here 1 to 4). Graph: each cell is linked to its row, column and box.

coin chainSudoku coin↔cell face we see↔given digit probability of A or B↔probability of each digit
So4 × 4: 7 neighbours per cell; 9 × 9: 20. A filled cell tells its neighbours “not my digit”.NextWhat does a cell hold, and what replaces each part of our network?
7 · One application: Sudoku · The parts

Every part of our network has a Sudoku version

A coin held one score, leaning to A or B. A cell holds four probabilities, one per digit; a given digit starts at certainty.

partcoin chain Sudoku

7 · One application: Sudoku · Rounds

Round 2 uses what round 1 decided: reach grows by one cell

Round 1 settled the blue cell. The cell to its right heard only 1 and 2 in round 1; in round 2 it also hears the new 4.

SoA deduction travels one link per round : hard puzzles need chains of deductions, so many rounds.NextHow does the network learn the rules?
7 · One application: Sudoku · Training

Training: solved puzzles are the targets

As in Part 1 : a practice puzzle, its solution as the targets, the network’s output, a small change to the parameters θ\thetaθ. Nobody tells the network the rules.

SoThe message network learns “a 1 next door rules out 1” because that shrinks the gap on thousands of solved puzzles.NextWhy does one network solve every puzzle?
7 · One application: Sudoku · Symmetry

Swap two rows: the same graph, so the outputs swap along

Rows 1 and 2 share the same boxes, so swapping them only renumbers the cells . Every cell keeps its neighbours.

SoBy the theorem of Part 2 , each cell keeps its four probabilities: one network for every puzzle, and for 9 × 9 as for 4 × 4.NextHow well does it work, and where does it stop?
7 · One application: Sudoku · Result

Result: 96.6% of the hardest puzzles, and two limits we predicted

  1. Result. Trained on solved puzzles, the network solves 96.6% of the hardest 9 × 9 Sudokus in its test set [Sudoku].
  2. Limit 1, reach (Part 4). A deduction travels one link per round; hard puzzles need long chains, so many rounds.
  3. Limit 2, what it sees (Part 5). Two blank cells with the same computation tree get the same four probabilities: no guessing between them.

One graph, one learned message, every part of today at work.

SoSudoku used a graph we chose by hand.NextWhat graph does a language model use?
7 · Sudoku, then language models · · the graph

A sentence is a graph: every word linked to every word

Sudoku linked a cell to its row, column and box. A language model does not know in advance which words matter to which, so it links every pair: the complete graph, each word also linked to itself.

Sonnn words give n⋅nn\cdot nn⋅n links; which links matter must be decided per sentence.NextWhich of the three message rules decides links per input?

2 symmetryoutputs follow the coins outputs follow the words: “dog bites man” = “man bites dog” unless the position is an input: positional encoding

4 depthTTT layers reach TTT linksevery word is 1 link from every word: one layer reaches all; the cost is n2n^2n2 weights per layer
5 limitequal computation trees, equal outputswithout positions, two words with the same neighbours are identical; positions break the tie
SoEvery result of today applies; Lecture 12 builds the Transformer from here.NextWhat should we remember?
Summary · The network

One network, five results

Each part answered one question about the same learned network.

Derive the messages when the factors are known; otherwise, learn them from examples. A Transformer is this network on the complete graph.

Check yourself

Check yourself (1 of 3): Parts 1 and 2

1. Belief propagation starts from the face probabilities. In a graph neural network, which learned part replaces this start?
Answer. The embedding: the learned start; for us the score u⋅xiu\cdot x_iu⋅xi​ from the face.
2. We swap the numbers of two coins of a chain. The graph neural network’s output for a given coin …
Answer. Stays the same: a sum ignores order, so each output moves with its coin.

Learned parts replace fixed formulas; numbering never matters.

Check yourself

Check yourself (2 of 3): Parts 3 and 4

3. Node 2 has three friends; only friend 1 carries a signal. Which network can give friend 1 the largest weight?
Answer. Graph attention: its weights are computed from the scores; the others use only degrees or sample size.
4. We go from 4 to 6 layers on 20-coin chains. The floor, TTT rounds of belief propagation, goes …
Answer. Down: each coin sees two more links, which can only help; 0.0085 to 0.0024.

Learned weights pick useful neighbours; more layers see further.

Check yourself

Check yourself (3 of 3): Part 4’s cost and Part 5

5. We apply 40 averaging layers without parameters. The coins’ scores become …
Answer. More alike: each average mixes neighbours; the spread fell from 2 to 0.083.
6. Can more layers separate a ring of six from two triangles, all faces H?
Answer. No: every coin’s computation tree is the same at every depth.

Depth makes nodes alike; equal trees stay equal.

What's next

Next: a toy weather model, then amortized inference

ProblemOne network handles every chain at once.We doFriday: a small weather model. Lecture 10: this idea, named.WhyTraining once serves every new input.
SoA network that outputs a posterior for any data is amortized inference.NextWhen is such a network good enough?

Appendix · A bigger network · Why a list

One list per coin must hold more than two chances

Belief propagation stores a message for each direction of a link; a graph neural network stores only one list per coin.

SoCoin 2’s list also holds what coin 1 sent, so it needs room. Its length is our choice; ours is 16 .NextHow do we write one round of the network?
Appendix · A bigger network · Worked example

On our chain, the network misses each answer by under 0.01

We give the trained network the faces H H T H T and compare its chance of A for each coin with the exact one. Coin 1: 0.712 against 0.715, a gap of only 0.003.

SoThe largest gap is 0.0099 (coin 3), although the network never saw the coin model itself.NextHow does the network get coin 3’s 0.515?
Appendix · A bigger network · Worked example

Inside the network: each layer, coin 3 hears one coin further

Follow coin 3’s list h3h_3h3​ through the network . The embedding starts it from the face T; each layer adds what the two neighbours send .

SoAfter two layers the list holds all five faces, as in belief propagation ; layers 3 and 4 refine them. The readout gives 0.515.NextWhere else do learned messages already help?
